To rifle through something means to search through it quickly, roughly, and carelessly — usually tossing items aside, creating disorder — in order to find something specific or steal valuables.

The key feeling the word captures is urgent, messy searching. It is not calm or careful. It is fast and disruptive.

Imagine a burglar who breaks into a house. They don't neatly inspect each drawer. They yank it open, dump the contents, fling things around, and move to the next one. That is rifling. Or picture yourself frantically digging through your own bag, throwing things aside, desperate to find your phone before a call ends. That is also rifling.

The action always involves:

  • Speed — it is hurried, not leisurely
  • Disorder — things get moved, overturned, or scattered
  • A goal — you are looking for something specific

No. The word can describe someone going through their own belongings when they are in a hurry. But when used about someone searching another person's belongings, it almost always carries a sense of intrusion, violation, or theft. The tone shifts accordingly.

Compare:

  • "She rifled through her own suitcase, looking for her passport." — hurried, slightly chaotic, no moral judgment
  • "The thief rifled through her suitcase." — intrusive, violating, clearly wrong

The word itself does not require theft, but context often makes the intent clear.
How It Is Used in Sentences

You will almost always see "rifle" followed by "through" and then the thing being searched:

  • He rifled through the files on the desk, looking for the contract.
  • She rifled through her purse but couldn't find her keys.
  • The soldiers rifled through the villagers' homes.
  • I rifled through every drawer but the receipt was gone.

Occasionally, you will see it used without "through" — "He rifled the cabinet" — but "rifle through" is far more natural and common.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Rifle" is slightly more vivid and forceful than saying "search through" or "look through." When a writer chooses this word, they are signalling: this was not a gentle or organized search. It was urgent, rough, and disruptive.

It sits between two similar words:

  • Rummage — also means to search messily, but feels more casual and less aggressive (rummaging through a sale bin, rummaging for snacks)
  • Ransack — means to search while causing serious destruction and chaos, usually implying a thorough act of plunder (an army ransacks a city)

"Rifle" lands in the middle — more forceful than rummaging, less destructive than ransacking.

There is a second, more technical verb sense: to rifle a gun barrel means to cut spiral grooves inside the barrel. These grooves make a bullet spin as it travels, which greatly improves its accuracy and range. This is where the noun "rifle" (the gun) comes from — it is a gun with a rifled barrel.

You will almost never encounter this verb meaning in everyday reading or conversation. It appears in military history, ballistics, or gunsmithing contexts. If you see "rifle" used as a verb in a novel, newspaper, or conversation, it is virtually always the first meaning — searching roughly.

Whenever you see "rifle through," ask yourself: someone is searching something fast and messily, probably looking for something specific, possibly without permission. That is the full picture. The word packages speed, disorder, purpose, and often a hint of intrusion — all in a single verb.
